newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Oct 30.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Oct 30.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- CARADON DIRECTOR UNDER SCRUTINY

Institutional shareholders of Caradon, the building materials company, have expressed concern about Trefor Llewellyn's role as finance director after a six year period as finance director of disgraced do-it-yourself retailer Wickes. Llewellyn, who joined Caradon in August last year after leaving Wickes, claims to have no knowledge of the true nature of the rebate arrangements at Wickes, and has agreed to pay back the bonus paid to him by Wickes in 1995. On that basis the company has agreed to make no claim against him.
-- BUNDESBANK FEAR AS FRANCE FAILS MAASTRICHT TEST

The Bundesbank yesterday warned that Germany is unlikely to hit the rigid debt and deficit targets set out by the Maastricht Treaty as a condition for entering into monetary union. The warning came just a few hours before a European Union committee rejected the French government's plans for budget cuts to meet the Maastricht criteria. It is highly unlikely that France will satisfy membership conditions by 1997.
-- CLARKE POISED TO HOLD RATES UNTIL THE BUDGET

Despite credit figures showing the strength of the economy, the Chancellor Kenneth Clarke is expected to leave interest rates unchanged following today's monthly policy meeting between himself and Eddie George, the governor of the Bank of England. Clarke is expected to hold back on rates until after next month's Budget.
THE TIMES
-- OFWAT DEMANDS PRICE CURB AS DIVIDENDS SOAR

The water industry regulator, Ofwat, yesterday warned water companies to curb prices next year following a series of large shareholder payouts and lower than expected spending on pipelines. Ian Byatt, Director General of Water Services stated that companies that had deviated from spending plans submitted in the last pricing review should not raise water prices to the limit allowed under the present regulatory system. He also made clear his disapproval of dividend payments from the regulated business to the parent group which are in excess of what is needed to meet the cost of capital.
-- THAMES WATER INCREASES INTERIM PAYOUT 22 PERCENT

Thames Water lifted its interim dividend by 22 percent yesterday on the same day the industry regulator issued a stern warning that companies should justify their payouts. Thames said that the increased payment has been brought about by a reduction in the number of shares from a share buy-back programme, as well as a contribution to profits from non-regulated businesses and good profit growth.
-- PIPELINE PROMISES NORTH SEA JOBS BOOST

The Government yesterday approved the construction of a pipeline to Bacton in Norfolk from three new oil and gas fields. The Shell group estimate that the British offshore construction industry would benefit to the tune of 4,000 man years. British Gas will be disappointed by the decision as they had lobbied hard to land the gas in the North of England.
THE GUARDIAN
-- FUND MANAGER'S 'WRONG BOX' MISTAKE CAUSES CHAOS

A fund manager at US investment giant Heine Securities caused chaos during last month's 250 million break-up bid for the GT Chile Growth Fund when he "ticked the wrong box" in the formal share offer from predator, Recent Pacific. He pledged support for the bid rather than for the alternative cash offer, like the majority of former GT shareholders. One source said last night that Heine was to blame for creating the most complicated deal of 1996.
-- SWISS BANK SUBSIDIARY FACES FRAUD CHARGES

Jersey police have charged Cantrade Private Bank Switzerland, a Union Bank of Switzerland subsidiary based in the Channel Islands, with fraud. Charges are being brought against the bank and one of its currency dealers, Peter Stoneman, as well as a former partner of Touche Ross accountants, over currency dealing transactions worth up to 17.5 million pounds stg.
-- PROTON TO TAKE OVER LOTUS WITH 50 MILLION POUNDS RESCUE PACKAGE

Proton, the Malaysian car company, is to take over Lotus in a 50 million pounds stg rescue bid. The move will bring Lotus, the Norfolk-based sports car and engineering company, from the brink of bankruptcy and represents Proton's most significant step in its plans for European expansion to date.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- SECRET PIA DOCUMENT NAMES BIGGEST PENSIONS OFFENDERS

Documents obtained by the Independent newspaper show that Prudential, Pearl, Legal & General and the TSB are among 26 companies that have contributed almost three-quarters of the 560,000 mis-sold pensions now under review. The review details were overseen by the Personal Investment Authority at a meeting earlier this month and the figures were thought so sensitive that those present were asked to hand back their copies to be destroyed.
-- ANGLO BUYS OUT BOCK FOR 257 MILLION POUNDS

Anglo-American, the South African conglomerate yesterday bought Dieter Bock's 18.3 percent stake in Lonrho for 257 million pounds stg. Bock then announced that he is standing down as chief executive of the mining to hotels group ahead of its forthcoming demerger. Nicholas Morrell, previously deputy managing director at Lonrho, will replace Bock. Anglo-American now have a 26 percent shareholding in Lonrho.
-- ZENECA SEES SHARES DIP DESPITE SURGE IN SALES

Shares in Zeneca, the drugs group, slid 38.5p to 17.11 pounds stg yesterday despite the announcement of a 14 percent surge in sales to 4.1 billion pounds stg for the first nine months. The whole pharmaceuticals sector was hit amid fears that President Clinton's healthcare reforms could be revived after next weeks's US election.
